result:
There’s a peculiar magic in the in-between—not the destination, not the origin, but that suspended breath where one thing has ended and another hasn’t begun. The gray half-light before sunrise, when streetlamps still glow but the sky has turned blue. The train platform at dawn, empty except for coffee steam and the distant hum of an approaching engine. These are liminal spaces, and we rush through them as if they were errors in the itinerary.

We are obsessed with arrival. We measure lives in milestones—graduations, promotions, retirements—as if existence were doors slamming behind us. But most of living happens in the corridors: the conversation that goes nowhere, the unfinished manuscript, the years between who you were and who you’re becoming, which have no name.

I’ve come to cherish these unremarkable thresholds. The airport at midnight, fluorescent and strange, where everyone is temporarily nobody’s neighbor. The Sunday afternoon belonging neither to leisure nor to Monday’s obligations. Even grief has its liminal phase, that strange numbness before sharp edges arrive.

Perhaps these moments feel vivid because they strip away our roles. Without the script of “work” or “success,” we are just consciousness, briefly unassigned. It can be unsettling. We reach for phones, for certainty. But if we stay still, there’s freedom in not knowing what comes next.

The world rewards clarity and five-year plans. Yet some of the most honest parts of being human occur when the map runs out. So I try to walk slower through doorways now. I notice the quality of light in parking garages, the silence of snow before anyone walks on it. These aren’t wasted moments. They are the texture of a life that refuses to be only its highlights.
